description: Beginners run group exercises and games that drill the core 'Yes, And' agreement principle, focusing on impulse, spontaneity, listening, and being present in the moment.

Students create characters through internal motivations (point of view, status, wants & intentions) and external choices (physicality, relationships), then play scenes that clearly establish the 'who'.
Students place character work into full scenes covering who/what/where, beginnings & middles, platforms, and an intro to tilts/routine breaks (the turn that escalates a scene).
Classic Viola Spolin-based games and side-coaching exercises (ensemble, who/what/where, creating from abundance) used to build emotional intelligence and discovery-based play.
Students study and analyze classic Second City sketches from the archives to learn the theater's satirical styles and genres.
Seven-week course where students improvise songs on the spot, drilling melody building, rhyming, and structuring simple and complex improvised songs.

exercise_name: Stand-Up set creation & open mic prep
description: Students write and workshop their own solo comedy material, learn joke construction, craft a set, and learn how to navigate their first open mic; course ends in a showcase.

Students bring structure and craft to autobiographical stories, develop their point of view, generate from abundance, and build a collection of personal stories; culminates in an out-of-class performance. Weekly hybrid format mixes self-paced assignments with live group workshops and feedback.
Weekly sketch-writing assignments where students write material, share it with the class, and receive instructor feedback in a hybrid self-paced + live format.

The signature UCB exercise: establish a Base Reality via 'Yes, And', identify and frame the First Unusual Thing, justify it ('if this is true, why is it true?'), then heighten it 3-5 times via If/Then ('if this is true, what else is true?'), ending once the game is fully heightened.
Players practice 'framing' — explicitly letting a scene partner know that they said or did something unusual within the base reality, so both performers can build it into the game.

Beginners drill listening, character agreement, character development and status, object/environment work, 'playing at the top of your intelligence', and heightening through games building up to two-person scenes.
Students drill group games, heightening them with specifics (e.g. 'gangsta figure skater' — play the specifics of gangstas AND figure skating), via walk-ons and tag-outs.
Students drill Harold beats: first beats establish a game, second beats narrow focus and replay the game, third beats heighten and connect scenes by game/theme/plot.

exercise_name: Improv openings (Pattern Game, Invocation, Monologues, Organic Opening)
description: Students practice Harold openings: the Pattern Game (free-associate words/ideas into a pattern), the Invocation (build an idea up via escalating address forms), character/personal monologues, and organic openings to generate scene material.
Capstone: students perform full Harolds (an opening, three two-person scene beats, and group games connected by theme/game) in class and in a class show.

Weekly writing assignments where students write sketches in different formats and read them aloud as a class: character sketches, commercial parodies (change one thing), genre parodies (3-5 pages), and political/topical sketches that 'take it to the extreme'. Each sketch develops a single premise, one game, heightened stakes, and an epiphany.
Students learn pitching, brainstorming and desk pieces, then develop a 3-sketch packet of their strongest work and receive 1:1 teacher feedback on it.
Students apply game-of-the-scene principles to improvised songs, drilling musical scene structure.

Take a random sentence/headline and ask: (1) what is assumed/expected that I can shatter? (2) is there a double-entendre / alternate meaning? (3) can two dissimilar ideas converge into a juxtaposition list? Then write joke variations off each answer.

Repeat a single line aloud (e.g. 'Let me help you with your baggage'), stressing a different word each time, and write a joke response for each emphasis — surfacing multiple comedic angles from one sentence. A no-performance 'wax-on/wax-off' instinct-builder.

Generate jokes from one subject using five angles: (1) create an analogy to an unrelated concept, (2) add a descriptor/weakness to the subject, (3) research real facts and riff on them, (4) define the subject and contrast definitions, (5) reform a cliché/take-off with an unexpected ending.
Start with a single subject and rapidly list out associations/concepts to flesh out material, then mine the list for joke premises.

exercise_name: Write 15 jokes from a headline in 30 minutes
description: Speed-writing demo/exercise: take a Yahoo News headline and rapidly generate ~15 jokes in 30 minutes by applying the clinic's joke-structure formulas (assumption-shattering, double meaning, juxtaposition).

exercise_name: Joke Writing 1-2-3 / Breaking Comedy's DNA system
description: A structured joke-writing framework (downloadable workbook + 'Breakthrough Comedy Writing System') that breaks jokes into setup/premise/punchline with formulas for building act-outs and tags. Used as a self-study lead magnet and in the 8-week class.

exercise_name: Joke Your Way Through Life joke-writing challenge
description: A guided joke-writing challenge (email/funnel-based) prompting participants to write jokes on a schedule using the clinic's methods.
Live 8-week class where students write material from scratch using the clinic's formulas, workshop it, and build toward a stand-up set / open mic.
Beginners learn the fundamentals of improvisation through fast-paced games and exercises that lay the foundation for the Groundlings style of improv and sketch.
Students design well-rounded improv characters and develop the Groundlings' signature character work through improvised scenes and solo character monologues.
Using skills from Basic, students concentrate on scene work and the Groundlings' character development inside improvised scenes and monologues.
Expanded character development and advanced scene work combining improv and writing exercises, culminating in an improv performance on the Gary Austin Stage.
Six-session sketch course teaching the difference between character and premise sketches, identifying beats, writing for the medium, and how to find material.
Stress-free ~2.5 hour single-session introduction to improv via games and exercises, open to anyone with no experience, taken from home.

Beginners build improv fundamentals through exercises, games, and storytelling grounded in acceptance, agreement, honesty, connections, listening, and commitment, culminating in learning and performing iO's signature long-form, The Harold.

'Performer's skill set' — games and exercises building strong/bold/committed character choices, physicality, environment, and stage picture to get the improviser out of their head and into the world onstage.

Extensive two-person scene work sharpening listening, emotional/authentic choices, status, and 'game', plus editing techniques — tag-outs and walk-ons — with more Harold practice. Philosophy: 'every line is golden'.
Students build character, relationship, and form across classic long-form structures, with grounded scene work as the foundation and continued emphasis on The Harold.
Advanced students collaboratively devise an entirely original long-form piece and then perform it on iO's stage for eight consecutive weeks, becoming eligible to audition for House Teams.
iO's curriculum derives from the Del Close / Charna Halpern 'Truth in Comedy' manual — group mind, finding the game, heightening, and the Harold structure are practiced as the theater's core method.
Three-level 'undergraduate' fundamentals track; Level 1 introduces game-based long-form improv basics through scene work.
A drop-in workshop combining the opening, premise initiation, and game play — students repeatedly drill establishing a premise and playing the game of a scene.
Two-person scenes performed for detailed instructor feedback/notes — students run scene after scene and get coached on patterns.
Extended scene practice with detailed feedback and pattern-focused coaching, where students adjust based on notes between reps.
Will Hines's Monday class where students do a high volume of scenes and receive detailed individual notes on each.
Saturday/Sunday morning open-level drop-in classes (no pre-registration) led by rotating teachers, mixing exercises and scene practice.
Community practice formats: a weekly open jam, Draft Night events, and multi-day-a-week 'Bitness' classes to build consistent reps in a low-stakes setting.
Advanced 'grad school' classes teaching cutting-edge improv theory, open to anyone who has taken a couple of long-form classes anywhere.
